title: The first Aura Seeker IR Pokémon cards are here, and they might actually be TOO pretty
content:
What sets an SIR Pokémon card apart from an IR? Is it just rarity, the chance of pulling one from a pack? Or should an SIR card be instantly identifiable as special.- before you check the card's rarity symbol?

I only ask, because the first secret rare cards from the Japanese Pokémon set Aura Seeker (our Flowing Fists) have been revealed, and look - it's not that I think the Secret Illustration Rare for Mega Lucario Z looks bad - it's just that the other cards, taken as a whole, blow it out of the water.

Mostly I'm looking at the Blatoise and Hatterene cards here, which I personally think could pass for SIRs easily. While there's nothing that unique about this depiction of the big blue Kanto starter, the close-up makes the turtle super imposing, and the environment look lush. With the sun blazing white and the water's reflections shining on the Pokémon, that is one good-looking scene.

Hatterene is the standout of this little quartet. The high contrast, colorful, heavily patterned art style looks super unique and the fairy/psychic type just shines on this card.

Meanwhile the Lucario Z is… well, I think it's going to be contentious. It's got the highly textured look that the Pokémon TCG likes for its chase SIR cards nowadays (see Darkrai, Rayquaza etc) but the colors are pretty muted and it's pretty hard to see what's going on. Is Lucario in a battle here? Admittedly, you couldn't really see what was going on in the Rayquaza Delta Reign or Darkrai Pitch Black SIRs either, but those were more deliberately abstract. Here, we see terrain and ripples of psychic energy, but not the whole scene.

It's a good card, but is it obviously an SIR next to that Blastoise and that Hatterene? I'd say no, but what do you think?

title: GTA VI's 'biggest' actor is making a miniature wargame
content:
Tommy Rice is the biggest actor to work on GTA VI, in the sense that he is only slightly smaller than a Kodiak bear. I met him in person at Adepticon earlier this year, taller and more physically imposing than the Space Marine cosplayers wearing their foam power armor and plasterer's stilts. A body-builder, former NFL-hopeful, actor, and author, he was at the massive miniature wargaming convention to demonstrate the miniature wargame, Partha Wars, which he is developing in partnership with Catalyst Game Labs. Last week he revealed that he was also the mocap artist for GTA VI's massive body-building NPC Nate Bozer; that was all the excuse I needed to call him up and find out what it was like to be part of the biggest event in gamer culture in a generation, and check in on Partha Wars' development to boot.

Rice was invited to test for a part in GTA VI way back in 2022. He remembers when his agent told him about the gig: "she's like, Well, you're going to be this big guy… the way that she described it, I thought it was Lord of the Rings, like a cave troll." He twigged to what the job actually was when he got the casting script. He auditioned, and early in 2023 he got the news that he'd booked the part: "it just floored me".

Nate Bozer doesn't feature in the story until act 4, but you'll likely see Rice's performance a lot earlier. "When I wasn't playing Nate, they would pull me aside and I would be big characters, anytime you see someone big robbing a bank, that could be me". He was also the subject matter expert on weight lifting: "everything you lift, I had a hand in making sure the form was good, stuff like that".

Though he's had his copy of GTA VI for a couple of weeks, it's a big game, and he still hasn't gotten to see his main performance in act IV. Comedian Brendan Sagalow provided Bozer's voice - "we made the perfect fun character", Tommy says. He remembers a great take working with Manni L. Perez, for the scene where Bozer is training weights with protagonist Lucia Caminos: "I dropped down on all fours and I was like, Come on girl, ruff ruff ruff! Bark like a dog, let's go, lift that weight! - we were laughing so hard".

Partha Wars

Partha Wars takes its setting from Rice's science-fantasy novel The Lok, a world where dragons dog-fight with fighter jets and rune-armored Spartans go toe to toe with Orcs in power armor. It's being developed at Catalyst Game Labs, best known as the home of Battletech. Its reveal at Adepticon 2026 was very low-key, a tiny stall bolted onto the side of the huge Battletech booth, and I only spotted it thanks to the gorgeous miniatures (and the game designer the size of a telephone booth).

The minis are all the work of veteran miniature sculptor Javier Ureña. "It's pretty cool to see such a beautiful miniature designer doing stuff that's in my head", Rice says, "the miniatures look phenomenal, more so than when you saw them". Four factions have now been fleshed out, and Rice teases me that he has a 3D render of a dragon on his computer.

Release plans are still up in the air, but a Kickstarter launch some time in 2027 seems likely. "The starter set will have two main factions… and something that you can use in your other factions, too, because the battle suits are basically mercenaries, you can get the chassis and use them in any army". Some of the miniatures have already gone on sale as convention exclusive, "a new Spartan running with a spear and a tinkerbot, which is a little Spartan robot", plus a new battle suit design. Stock sold out at GenCon, but more will be available at Pax Unplugged.

The material that the miniatures will be made from hasn't been finalized, but it "should be the better material" that Catalyst has access to - Rice isn't sure of the trade name. They're being designed to be supplied "assembled, but then you can swap heads or swap weapons", and for converters "we might be doing a sprue separately" with more components.

Then there's the rulebook. I read the alpha rules after Adepticon and thought they needed work, but they already gave a good sense of the game's identity: there's a big focus on momentum, weight, and kinetic combat, just right for a game with such heroically chunky miniatures. Rice assures me "the rules have been crunched, the lore is huge and all-encompassing but it's been fleshed out so that it's better for the rule book… that'll be done in the next few weeks".

While the game will launch with four factions, the setting has twelve, and Rice says he's fighting his own enthusiasm to keep things in scope. "I want to do big things with it", he says, "I'm super, super excited about what we're about to do with it - really pumped". Which is just the kind of statement I expect from this man: a nerd living his best nerdy life, heading forwards with all the momentum (and approximate body mass) of a freight train.

To learn more about Partha Wars, here's my original preview of the game from Adepticon 2026.

If you happened to pick up a Partha Wars miniature at GenCon and want to show it off, or you just want to chat about niche wargames, you're welcome in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: New Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War IV trailer teases Chaos Space Marines as the fifth faction
content:
On Monday King Art Games, developer of the upcoming Warhammer 40k: Dawnof War IV, has just dropped a new trailer for the game. Designed to drum up sales for the game's deluxe Commander Edition, for experienced tabletop Warhammer 40k fans it also has a pretty clear hint about the first new faction arriving in DLC - it looks like we're getting Chaos Space Marines.

Dawn of War  4 Commander Edition comes with some perks, including unlocking the game three days early, getting the in-game soundtrack, and a subscription game to all the DLC released during year one. Two pieces have already been announced, Prologue and Aftermath, and the trailer gives us a few more morsels of information.

In the Story Prologue, you'll "return to Aurelia, the lost homeworld of the Blood Ravens, as a legendary commander leads a strikeforce in search of something vital for the chapter's future". The smart money is on Chapter Master Gabriel Angelos, because who else counts as a legendary commander of the Blood Ravens? He was the protagonist in DoW and DoW 3, and then the commander in DoW 2 was a nameless player insert.

Aurelia is really not a place you want to go unless you have good reason: it was yanked into the warp by the Great Unclean One Ulkair, and spat back into reality through the machinations of the Black Legion. Now "beneath its ruins, something awaits, something that will change the Blood Ravens forever".

The store description for the Aftermath DLC has already confirmed it will add a new playable faction "across all game modes" and "a story-driven campaign continuation" of the Kronus narrative from the main game. There'll also be "new playable commanders".

But who will the fifth playable faction be? There's a clue in the trailer. Just as Toby Longworth booms out that "what began on Aurelia is coming to Kronus", we get a three second shot of a pair of glowing, perfectly circular yellow eyes, shrouded in ember-flecked smoke. Jagged lines of light emanate out from around the eyes, as if the entity is burning from within, and the light is shining through a cracked mask.

Warhammer 40k has a surprising number of malignant entities that glow with an inner light, but only one has such perfectly circular, lens-like eyes: Vashtorr the Arkifane, the Soul Forge King, the Chaos demigod of "unrestrained invention and abominable artifice".

Vashtorr is a greater daemonic entity that has so far remained independent from the main four 40k Chaos Gods. It often cooperates with the Chaos Space Marines, particularly the Black Legion, joining in Abaddon the Despoiler's black crusades, and the Iron Warriors, with whom it shares an affinity for cramming unwilling daemons into mechanical bodies to create daemon engines.

I'm genuinely hyped to see how the team at King Art Games animate the Chaos Space Marines and particularly the daemon engines. Since they last appeared in Dawn of War 2 the model range for more or less the entire Warhammer 40k faction has been refreshed, and the new sculpts are sick - I really want to see how the new Defiler scuttles across the battlefield!

How are you feeling about Dawn of War 4 - does it look like it'll knock Space Marine 2 from its spot as the best Warhammer 40k game ever, or are you worried about how a modern RTS can live up to your nostalgic memories of the original game? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Narrative Forge: Five Leagues from the Mortal Realms - Part 2
content:
Our “Narrative Forge” hobby articles exist to encourage stretching yourself out in the hobby - and that includes trying new games and rules. But those can be quite a commitment... unless you use what you already have! In this follow up to the first Five Leagues From The Mortal Realms, Hydriatus gets his campaign underway!

Welcome back readers, to our look at trying out Five Leagues from the Borderlands with your Age of Sigmar collections! After a lot of rolls on random tables to determine our cast and setting, we can begin the tale of Vizhna the Warqueen, on a quest to uncover the secrets of a strange map she found whilst raiding in the realm of Ghur...

Hakkafjord

Though considered one of the "lesser" fjords of Bloodwhiten, it is also one of the most accessible. It was popular with the pirates and smugglers of the Splitneck Sea for ages, who established the small port of Khulin as a refuge from the agents of the Order of Azyr based out of Wreathport. In fact, the search for Khulin was one of the factors that led to the founding of Coldfort.

In the years since the Dawnbringer Crusades brought the Sigmarites to Bjarl, not all have held fast to their faith. The ever-present winter of the southern continent wears away at the strongest resolves, and one can always hear the whispers of the Dark Gods upon the wind. So it came that a successful merchant out of Wreathport found themselves driven to ruin through the machinations of their rivals, and forced to flee. Having nowhere else to go, they sailed the Splitneck Sea until they came across the longships of the southern raiders.

But rather than surrender to them, he offered a parlay, and traded his knowledge of Wreathport and it's navy in exchange for a place amongst the corsairs. Bemused, they accepted, and the merchant was allowed to settle in their fledgling village. Once there, he set about establishing himself as a notable trader, using his old contacts in Wreathport and Coldfort to setup a successful smuggling operation. Soon enough, he had rebuilt his wealth, and used it to finance the construction of a home more befitting his status.

And so Frosthaven was founded, a place where the criminals and exiles from the Sigmarite strongholds could gather and live out their lives free from the tyranny of Azyr.

A quick trace of the region with defined Map Areas and placed locations.

Hakkafjord has the following locations:

  • Khulin (Village/Market Town).
  • Frosthaven (Town/Manor).
  • The Tomb of Tidedrinker (Delve).
  • An undiscovered location.
  • Drowned Barrows (Soulblight Gravelords Camp)
  • Draugr's Copse (Sylvaneth Camp)
  • Camp Shuang (Cities of Sigmar Camp)

The following locations are hidden:

  • The Delve detailed on the Ancient Map
  • A Soulblight Hideout
  • A Sylvaneth Hideout
  • A Cities of Sigmar Hideout

The threat levels of the region are:

  • Cities of Sigmar (6)
  • Sylvaneth (5)
  • Soulblight Gravelords (5)

Vizhna's Oath (and by extension, the campaign), is considered complete once the Hidden Delve is completely cleared.

Campaign Phases

The campaign elements of the game rely heavily on random tables and charts, and focus more on narrative than simulation - it always takes you one campaign turn to travel to any location on the map, for example.

There is also an option to play a tutorial battle before beginning your campaign, but I skipped it to get right into the action!

The First Phase

Your first campaign turn always involves your warband arriving in the region, starting on the edge of the map and traveling somewhere. As part of my narrative, it seemed logical for Vizhna and her companions to be sailing into port, so I chose Khulin as my destination and rolled to see if anything happened en route.

My result? See Something in the Distance - Add an Unexplored Location to the map. Interesting, seems the place is full of ruins or strange creatures!

Upon reaching the village, my warband could only really Lay Low, as they had too little wealth to Trade from the start (you always want some cash in your warband stash to pay for upkeep when you eventually go exploring the wilds). However, reaching the village did grant me 1 Adventure Point!

Oh right - Adventure Points are a currency used to uncover Hidden Locations, gain additional money, upgrade settlements, reduce the Threat Level an enemy faction poses, and promote Followers to Heroes. Whenever you want to achieve one of those options, you spend Adventure Points and roll 1D6 - if you roll under your spend, you succeed.

So, our campaign would see Vizhna having to establish herself in the region, amass 6 Adventure Points, and spend them to uncover the Hidden Delve indicated by her mysterious map.

Finally, I rolled to see what news and rumors reached my warriors  this phase - and got Monster Spotted In Region - Add a Hidden Monster Lair to the map.

Huh, I wonder what monster it is?

Picking up my dice, I flipped to the relevant table and rolled. I got Undead Construct, a giant, terrifying, difficult to kill monster that is way out my warband's league for now. I don't really have anything to fit that in my collection, so I decided to switch it out for something I do have - a war mammoth proxying for a Slaughterbrute! I look at the list for something with appropriate rules and settle for a Giant - big, relatively quick, and sends people flying with each blow.

A mammoth marches through the Ghurish blizzard. (Credit - Hydriatus)

And with that, the first campaign turn comes to an end.

With the map showing what was clearly the Bloodwhiten Fjords, Vizhna marched north to the coast, from where she and her companions bartered for passage to one of the settlements there. 

As the fishing boat navigated the waters of BloodWhiten, Asfrid spied a tattered banner fluttering in the wind half-way up the side of one of the fjords they passed. Though it may well have marked an entrance to some underground labyrinth, the Oathsworn chose to stay the course, and arrived in Khulin after a few days. 

Though the villagers were soft and too preoccupied with notions of wealth, the party nevertheless found their way to one of the communal halls. Amidst the hazy smoke and meagre warmth, they learned of the dangers plaguing the region - of patrols from Coldfort ranging ever northwards, of irate nature spirits haunting those who traveled too far from the settlements, and the restless dead that jealously guarded their treasures amidst the snowy peaks. 

Drifa, the most experienced in what could be passably termed as diplomacy, managed to convince the village elders to let the group stay for free in return for their services - for Khulin was short of warriors, and the capability for violence was always in demand. And so Vizhna's Oathsworn patrolled the streets of Khulin for several days, their leader fruitlessly seeking anyone who could tell her more about the map she held. 

Taulveg meanwhile learned of a great beast wandering the fjords that had claimed the lives of several hunters - a worthy challenge for the Oathsworn perhaps? 

The Second Phase

As there was no battle involved in the first campaign phase, I immediately jumped into the second. As my warband was beginning the phase in a settlement, I rolled on the settlement event table - and rolled Got In A Fight. This meant a member of my warband got into an argument with the locals, and would have to pay reparations of 2 gold. Alternatively, I could sacrifice ALL my Activities for the phase.

Ouch. Having some funds I chose to bear the cost, as otherwise I would have to pay 3 gold for my warband upkeep. This way, one of my activities could be Help the Town Guard which always covers upkeep costs in a settlement. Not a promising start, but what can you expect in a village aligned with Chaos worshipers?

(Also for fun, I randomly rolled to see which member of my warband was the one who had gotten into a fight, and it turned out to be Sigrunn. Of course the unproven warrior would be the one to kick off...)

With one activity left to pick this phase, I chose to have my warband Meet the Locals - which resulted in Vizhna and her cohort being offered a Contract! Contracts are basically randomly generated missions, ranging from delivering something from one settlement to another, escorting an NPC, retrieving a particular item, or fighting specific foes.

In this case, the common folk of Khulin approached the warband and offered them 2 Gold in exchange for chasing off a local threat. Some rolls on associated tables and we had a mission - play a Camp Raid scenario against a randomly determined foe within 3 Phases. Another die roll later and this foe was Strange Troops - well trained mercenaries unaffiliated with any of the local threats.

A little thought and the lore for this whole thing came into focus...

While the locals of Khulin held no fondness for the tribes of the tundra, they recognized their capability for violence - and so offered them an opportunity to channel that in their favor. A band of pirates from across the Splitneck Sea had been causing trouble recently, and had setup camp just on the outskirts of the village - if they could be driven off, the village elders would part with some meager jewels Vizhna and her band could trade for supplies somewhere else.

Since I have been working on a Black Death City/Mordheim gang, I decided to grab those models and use them as a band of wealthy privateers lying low in Khulin and extorting the locals.

Privateers of the Splitneck Sea. (Credit - Hydriatus)

The First Battle

A Camp Raid scenario sees the warband sneaking up on their enemies from a blind spot, getting free movement until the enemy spots them. The enemy in this case consisted of 9 models - 5 melee, 2 ranged, a lieutenant, and a Scheming Heretic. Whilst Strange Soldiers have somewhat daunting stat-lines, being a Roadside Threat enemy meant that I only had to kill 6 of them to force the rest to flee. The key then would be to overwhelm them with unfair numerical matchups!

Vizhna's Chosen ready to raid! (Credit - Hydriatus)

As a raid scenario, this game started with an opportunity for my models to sneak up on the enemy - which they did, with Ikherd and Taulveg moving to flank the camp and intercept the returning sentries while Vizhna led the rest of the warband straight for the heart of the enemy.

After several careful moves, Drifa was detected, and the game began proper! And it very swiftly went downhill for my poor Darkoath!

Turn One.

Things started off alright, as I rolled six d6 for my warband, and assigned them to each model as their Initiative. If the die roll was equal to or below the model's Agility score, they would act first in the round. Then all the enemies would act, and then any model who had an initiative die higher than their Agility.

I had Ikherd activate first, and he successfully cast Distract on one of the ranged soldiers to waste their activation, while Vizhna, Drifa, and Asfrid made their way around the enemy camp to lure them out of position.

It turned out that the foe had someone amongst their ranks capable of enchanting my warriors, but Drifa shrugged off the attempt as she saw multiple enemies rushing back to threatened camp.

Turn Two.

Turn 2 started with some worse Initiative, but enough of my models got to activate before the enemy that I had a chance to trim their numbers. Drifa charged the closest spearman, and engaged in melee.

Combat in Five Leagues is always a one-on-one affair, covering three exchanges. You roll a d6 for each fighter and add their Combat skill and any modifiers such as being stunned or having a an ally within 1", and whoever rolls highest wins. If the charging model wins, it pushes the enemy back and rolls to see if their hit overcomes the target's Armour, and then another roll to see if the hit overcomes their Toughness.

Drifa managed to hit, break through the spearman's armour, but failed to overcome his Toughness - leaving him Wounded and Stunned. Despite these advantages, I just rolled poorly on the second exchange, and the spearman won, which meant he was the attacker for the final exchange - and managed to take Drifa completely out of action!

Smelling blood, Vizhna charged the wounded man next to finish him of, but again poor rolls saw her fended off. The bad luck continued when Taulveg activated and charged the war dog - only for it to win the first exchange, stun him on the second, and kill him on the third.

A poor start. And then it was time for the enemies to activate.

Ranged weapons always activate first, and while the formerly distracted gunner missed, the archer managed to land a truly impressive shot and Wound Vizhna (he needed a 6 on a d6 - forget bad luck, maybe I''m cursed). Then the wardog that had taken down Taulveg charged and took out Ikherd - but a soldier charged Sigrunn and failed their attacks, getting killed in turn on the following exchange!

Sadly, Sigrunn's victory was short lived as the charming Heretic struck her down right after, while a soldier and Lieutenant both engaged Vizhna, who only survived thanks to her shield!

The only surviving warband member with an activation left after all that was Asfrid, who charged in but was also repulsed with little difficulty.

The +1 to Combat the Strange Soldiers had was proving decisive!

Turn Three.

With things looking bleak, Vizhna used her Will point to Activate first, charging the wounded spearmen to try to force the enemy to take some Morale tests - but once again failed to beat him in melee.

Meanwhile, the gun-toting enemy rolled another 1 on their attack and so ran out of ammunition for the rest of the battle. Yay I guess? The Lieutenant and spearman both engaged Vizhna again but she managed to defend herself. The Heretic meanwhile stepped up and killed my other Follower.

Oh no.

Vizhna's last stand.

As the only hero left standing, Vizhna charged the Heretic to try to slay them and salvage some glory out of the whole debacle. But poor dice rolls struck again and she lost the first exchange, only to be taken out of action in the second!

...OK, maybe these Soldiers were less privateers and more Stormcast...

Post Game

Well, since I failed the scenario, I skipped the Loot and Experience sections and went straight to the Injury tables!

Vizhna rolled seriously injured, so expended her one Luck point to ignore that and miraculously escape harm.

Taulveg was only lightly injured, and needs 2 Phases to recover.

Drifa almost died, but a quick infusion of Silverleaf spared her that dark fate, though she would need 3 Phases to recover.

The Gods seem to be looking out for Ikherd, as he managed to just get knocked out by the vicious attack dog and made his way back to Khulin none the worse!

Sadly the Gods are fickle and both of my followers, the unblooded Alfrid and Sigrunn, died (even after I expended my last Silverleaf to try to save one of them)!

My warband's second week in Hakkafjord came to an end with it's numbers depleted to 2, coffers reduced to 4 gold, all my medical supplies used up, only two damaged weapons salvaged from the fallen for my troubles, and a single Adventure Point out of the six I needed.

Final Thoughts

And that's that! From here on, another Campaign Phase would begin, and Vizhna's Chosen would have to find a way to lick their wounds and rebuild their stash of supplies. A poor start for my poor warriors, but they were far from done with Hakkafjord... but that's a story for another time.

If you enjoyed this little story time, grab a copy of Five Leagues from the Borderlands, and see where your adventures in the Mortal Realms take you!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: MTG's ultimate Borg upgrade card spiked 600% in price since Star Trek launch
content:
It immediately caught my eye as one of the most interesting cards during MTG Star Trek spoiler season, and now Borg Cube has spiked drastically in price. Costing just $6.70 on Star Trek's official release day, November 13, the card has since risen 616% to a stomping $48.

Borg Cube is a seven mana spacecraft, but affinity for artifact creatures means it typically comes out much quicker. When it comes in it gets to exile something immediately, and then if you're able to station it up and get it attacking, it not only gives all your artifact creatures flying, but also lets you assimilate creatures bringing, them into the fold as part of your collective. It's a little slow, especially if you don't have a ton of artifacts around, but the potential upside is huge.

The main reason this card is spiking is that it's a really popular upgrade for the Borg MTG precon deck, 'We Are The Borg', led by The Borg Queen. In fact, it's a popular pick up with several of the legendary Borg creature cards (Borg Queen, Locutus, and Hugh First of Many) all three of which have proven more popular than Captain Kirk, according to EDHREC's numbers.

1/3

At first glance, a card like Borg Cube may not seem to be what 'We Are The Borg' really needs. It's a pretty slow deck out the box with an expensive seven mana commander that already does a bunch of assimilating for you. It's perhaps slightly overcosted removal which has the potential to become an out of control finisher.

However, this works a little awkwardly. The idea of attacking one turn to exile something and then attacking again the next to assimilate it sounds great, but if your opponents are letting this survive for multiple turn cycles they're doing something wrong. Instead, I think it's more valuable for letting you sail over the heads of your opponents' creatures and take someone out of the game. However, with a station cost of 12, you probably have to crew this thing up in stages, else you'll have a flying but totally tapped board that won't be able to swoop in for the win.

A sound addition or not, what the Borg Cube quite clearly is is a flavor win. This card fulfils the fantasy of playing the Borg better than perhaps any other MTG Star Trek card. It's big, scary, and isn't trying to hide.

What's your favorite Star Trek card? Let us know on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Necromunday: Orlock Ogryn Minders Model Review
content:
House Orlock recently received a slew of reinforcements, and among the other kits, the one that caught my attention immediately was the Ogryn Minders box. For the non-Brits among you, "minder" is a term in Cockney slang for a bodyguard, particularly one who guards a high-ranking member of the criminal underworld, so it's a perfect descriptor for these beefcakes. I am a real sucker for big lads (and lasses) like ogres and giants, so I just had to grab some when they became available to join my already burgeoning (though as yet, not completely painted) double-denim metalhead Orlock crew.

Orlock Ogryn Minders - Credit: keewa

The construction of each is pretty straightforward, with a front torso, back torso, and two legs forming the main trunk of the model, as you’d expect. Both poses are the same; the main difference is that one is wearing a T-shirt, while the other is shirtless (and ripped; these aren’t your flabby AOS Ogors, that’s for sure) under his sleeveless jacket, which has a nice big embossed Orlock sigil on the back. I like this sigil, but if you were hoping that you could build both Ogryns as sort of gang-neutral hangers-on, you’ll be disappointed; you have no choice but to take the piece with the large symbol, and it’ll be difficult to remove cleanly unless you’re an experienced modeller.

They tower over an ordinary Orlock ganger

Although each model is essentially the same, there are a healthy amount of options to customise them - each head is made of a combination of two pieces: a face (smug, yelling, and cigar chomping) and a top (bandana, goggles with bare head, goggles with Guile haircut, and goggles with bandana). Rather than being restricted to two pre-made heads, combining pieces to form a head allows for a good deal more customisation. This approach is pretty clever. It increases the amount of available options without also increasing the use of sprue real estate. My only real gripe with this is that the face of the cigar-chomper is in two pieces, with the jaw separate; it felt really unnecessary, and I honestly found it a bit fiddly to get it to sit just right.

Each leg has the option of three shin-pad designs, shared across both models, both scaled-up versions of familiar Orlock-style designs; four steel toe-caps, and the choice of three different belt-buckle/codpiece pieces, not an enormous amount of options to be sure, but enough that you could probably assemble two boxes’ worth and not have any look identical.

Arthur - Credit: keewa

In terms of armaments, one Ogryn can be outfitted with a pair of brass knuckles and a ripper gun slung across the back. The other (or both) can be outfitted with a ripper gun and a big melee weapon (choice between a very large spanner or a power maul – I chose the maul, but they both make excellent options and look great). If you go this second route, you only get one ripper gun being held in the hand; the other must be slung across the back, but to replace the gun-toting arm, you get an arm holding a cigar instead, which is neat! If you were feeling absolutely ridiculous, you could build an Ogryn so dedicated to smoking that he has a cigar in one hand and a cigar in his mouth. Completing the big lads are four appropriately Orlock-y armoured shoulder pads, though you don’t need to put any of them on at all if you don’t want to. The kit is very compact, in keeping with GW's recent design philosophy; they manage to squeeze quite a lot of bits onto a single sprue, but not so much that you can't get your clippers in between to get the pieces off the frame (looking at you, Militarum Tempestus Scions kit).

Terry - Credit: keewa

I had a lot of fun painting these; as with pretty much all the newer Necromunda kits, they're bursting with character, and you can really make them your own. The models are beautifully detailed, as sharp as any modern GW kit and go together easily. The designs fit in really well with those of the already established Orlock models (of which I am also very fond; I love me some House Springsteen, after all). If you’re a keen painter, like me, chances are you’ll find much to enjoy in these beefy boys.

At 36 euro (RRP) for two models, the Ogryn Minders are slightly cheaper than the Servitor Ogryns (which are also great). The price feels right; they are larger-than-normal, detailed models, and in any case, you’re unlikely to need that many of them; one look and the gang of your rivals will flee back into the underhive with their tails between their legs - if you're an Orlock player or someone who likes the Orlock aesthetic, you'll absolutely want to pick up a box; they're a no-brainer.

title: From the archives: Why Dungeons and Dragons doesn't need any more dragons
content:
This article was originally published on July 23, 2021.

By most accounts, dragons are pretty cool. Not in a chic, hip, down with the kids kind of way, but in the sense that they speak to all the best parts of fantasy fiction. Ferocious serpentines with massive wings and fire-breathing lungs, they appear in cultures the world over, and malleably fit the part of an evil beast that needs slaying, or an ancient monster terrorizing the region. They're big, evil, and immediately recognizable.

But they're not half overplayed. Ask any passerby to name a typical fantasy monster and, besides giving you a peculiar look, there's more than a good chance they'll say "dragon". The familiar flying lizards have saturated fantasy literature, film, and games for decades, becoming the go-to creature for a climactic battle or villainous pet.

Nearly all major fantasy franchises flirt with them. Smaug served as JRR Tolkien's beastly baddie in The Hobbit, George RR Martin posed them as medieval superweapons in A Song of Ice and Fire, and they're sprinkled across Harry Potter. Even John Tenniel's original illustration of Alice in Wonderland's Jabberwocky bore more than a passing resemblance to the Western interpretation: scaled body, bat-like wings, long tail, and four legs (albeit with a protruding neck and buck teeth for added flavor).

So when the final D&D sourcebook of the 2021 was unveiled to be Fizban's Treasury of Dragons, I wasn't filled with a wave of excitement. A tome that chronicles draconic history, magic, and lore, alongside providing additional GM resources for fielding dragons in your campaign, seems something of a missed opportunity. It's a safe bet on a vanilla RPG monster that doesn't warrant the spotlight, and overlooks the reams of more exciting opportunities just waiting for development.

Dragons undoubtedly work well for D&D. They're recognizable and clear-cut, letting DMs use them without having to explain vast amounts of lore to new players. You see a dragon, and you know what you're in for. But when I'm handed an all-encompassing fantasy system with which to develop original worlds and colorful characters, limited only by the boundaries of creativity, making dragons the focal point of that creation isn't much of a tempting offer.

They're too familiar, and pale in comparison to the weird and wacky creatures plastered across D&D's monster manual. What's a dragon's elegant form next to the bulbous blob of a Beholder, or its fiery breath next to the consciousness-destroying psychic powers of a Mind Flayer? I've seen a lot of dragons in fantasy fiction, and I'm sure that I'll see a lot more in the future, but D&D can do better.

The game's roster of monsters is impressive, spanning a huge variety of classic foes and niche enemies. Sillier picks, like the dreaded Grey Ooze, mashed creations, such as Jackalweres, and fan-favorites, such as Displacer Beasts, speak to the game's variety. There's an abundant supply of original, quirky monsters to explore, and D&D would do well to move beyond the tired fantasy focuses of other mediums - including those that it had a hand in popularizing.

Some might not buy my complaint. Outside of Fizban's, dragons rarely crop up in D&D adventures. But they're undoubtedly a staple of the game's visual presentation and popular perception. Both the D&D 5E Starter Set and Essentials Kit feature dragon encounters as focal moments of their adventures. Magic: The Gathering's D&D crossover set, Adventures in the Forgotten Realms, similarly placed a significant emphasis on notable dragon characters, and their various subraces.

Although they may not often appear in your homebrew campaigns or official D&D modules, dragons remain woven into the heart of the franchise. Fizban's Treasury of Dragons isn't some unexpected outlier, but a continuation of the game's emphasis on the classic monster.

Others might think I've been uncharitable. Dragons have served fantasy literature well over the decades, and D&D's dragons aren't merely a homogenous group. Evil Chromatic Dragons differ in motivation and mentality, Metallic Dragons have separate quirks and alignments, and the new Gem Dragons to be introduced to 5E in the upcoming sourcebook will undoubtedly bring more variety.

But, besides representing another point of bioessentialism, in which an entire race's moral compass and psychological temperaments are distilled to their physiological attributes, it's also not the case that these differences really count for much.

DMs might pick a particular subspecies that suits their campaign's theme, or use the contrasting attributes of dragons to make some narrative point. But, ultimately, they're still all dragons. They inspire similar reactions within players, and serve similar storytelling purposes. Heaping together a bunch of dragons of different colors doesn't stop them from simply being dragons.

So, forget dragons. I propose the next D&D sourcebook be dedicated to a more innovative monster; one that's still familiar, but vastly more creative. That most ridiculous of beasts: the humble Owlbear. Dragons might be gigantic fire-breathing lizards, but years of exposure has desensitized me to their ferocity. A three-meter tall feathered chimera, sporting nowt but a beak and razor-sharp claws, though - now that's scary stuff.

What's that you say? A game called Dungeons and Dragons could never so willfully dismiss the classic fantasy monster, which will forever hold a place of importance in the game? Well, I have a solution to that, too. I'm pleased to introduce Dungeons and Owlbears, the latest, revised edition of the world's biggest tabletop roleplaying game. Besides some minor balancing tweaks, it's exactly the same game you know and love, but with an endless supply of feathery mammals to encounter on your quests.

If alliteration is important, you may also consider the names Oubliettes and Owlbears, Occurrences and Owlbears, or Occasions and Owlbears. Please, take your pick in the knowledge that all options dramatically diminish draconic representation.

Look out for my next hot take, in which I'll be arguing why dungeons are an overplayed adventuring trope and should be replaced with more novel storytelling devices, such as rabbit holes, moral dilemmas, and metaphorical dream sequences.

Got a hot take of your own? Bring that spice to the official Wargamer Discord, where we discuss tabletop and its biggest news stories every day.

title: Subscribing to Tabletop Battles
content:
Tabletop Battles is your favorite worker-owned media collective covering news and gaming in the wargaming, boardgaming, and increasingly the videogaming space, and we'd like you to join our Patreon so we can keep doing what we do. Grand Theft Auto VI came out this week! I wrote a piece about the first day I spent with it. I also wrote a piece about Robert Pattinson as James Bond. All of my dumb thoughts will remain free, I can tell you that right now. To support those stupid thoughts, we have a variety of offerings.

Podcasts, Streaming, Video, No Ads

The first thing available on the $3 Every Bit Counts tier: No ads on the website. You go to the site, login through Patreon, and boom, they're gone, mobile and desktop. In addition, you get access to all our backer-exclusive podcasts, featuring the flagship offering HAMS Radio, where Rob and Norman talk about tabletop gaming (a lot of Trench Crusade recently, because Norman's our site lead on Trench Crusade), The Campaign Trail podcast which covers narrative campaign gaming, and anything else we decide to record a short series on. As a backer you can also hop into our livestreams whenever we're video gaming, like when Rob and Norman played through all of Boltgun 2 on stream recently.

Subscriber-Only Content

Let's talk about what else being a $10 Warhound Patron gets you. Three times a week, we go behind the paywall to get deep and functional about playing competitive tabletop Warhammer 40K. Sometimes this involves talking about army lists that are big in the meta right now. Sometimes we dive deeper on a new Codex release with theorycrafting and test game results, or react to how a new Codex is affecting competitive events before the next Dataslate. A favorite topic for our army-specific writers is talking about how they play into certain opponents, or how they handle teams play with their army and their list's disposition choice. Here's an example, written by Innes Wilson back in August, that talks about playing the Take and Hold disposition with Space Marines, complete with a pair of example army lists and how they work; I've pulled it out from behind the paywall.

Our subscriber-only articles are written by competitive players who have success on the table; Ben Jurek, Orks afficionado, Top 10 ITC finisher the last three years, member of Team USA and recent winner of the Utah Cup writes for us, as does Isaac Terada, Las Vegas Teams Tournament finalist, podium finisher for the Challenger's Cup and second place behind Ben at that Utah Cup. Two co-founders of Stat Check, teams specialist Jeremy Curie (Champion's Cup, Toronto Team Open and BFS team wins in 2025, many other podiums, judging experience) and the aforementioned Innes (Top 10 ITC the last six years, Rank 1 ELO, Rank 1 ITC, 6 UKTC super major wins, way too many event wins to succinctly name here) write subscriber-only pieces for us. And when it comes time to be competitive on the hobby side of the table, Rob "TheChirurgeon" Jones has a cabinet full of Best Painted wins in addition to taking World Championship qualifier tickets in 2025 and 2026 and winning the Ettin Tabledtalk GT in 2025. Seriously, there's an actual cabinet. He's running around Atlanta right now at the Grand Narrative, but he'll add to it soon.

The Tabletop Battles App

If you haven't downloaded the app yet, you can get it for free through one of the links below:

We've been running this app and its associated cluster of services for six years now, and it's in the best place it's ever been, with support for the current editions of Warhammer 40K, Warhammer 40K Kill Team, Warhammer Age of Sigmar, Warhammer Horus Heresy, Warhammer The Old World, and non-Games Workshop titles Conquest: The Last Argument of Kings and the StarCraft Tabletop Miniatures Game. There are a number of apps out there for this kind of thing, though; why use ours?

  • Runs faster and better. Tabletop Battles is built in Flutter and not React. Flutter is less common but removes a lot of runtime jank that can bog down React Native apps. If you've noticed that TTBA runs faster, this is a primary reason why. Flutter generally outperforms React Native and uses less CPU and as a result, less battery.
  • Built-in stats screens. If you want more than just a list of your games, we've got you covered, and we're working on more personal stats you can access via our Edge web app.
  • Faction trackers. If you want to track things like Pain tokens or Saga progress, our app has that.
  • Other game modes. Do you want to play asymmetric missions? Track custom games? Do you need a different disposition than the one you're allowed to select? The Tabletop Battles interface is much more flexible, and allows for custom score input.
  • Direct feedback. We read every bug report and work to implement changes, and we respond to inquiries on Discord. The Tabletop Battles app is very much what you help make it.

It's the best app on the market for logging your games, useful both at the table and as a historical record keeper, letting you track your game state during play and check how things went after the fact.

But whatever. That's what the plebs get. If you subscribe to the Tabletop Battles Patreon at the $5 level, you get access to Administratum, our narrative play engine. Administratum turns the Tabletop Battles App into your one stop solution for roster management, campaign tracking, and progression recording across any kind of ongoing  tournament or narrative event. It used to be that Administratum was only designed to work with the Crusade 40K narrative play mode, but much like Crusade, that's a thing of the past -- with Administratum 4.0, you can use all of its tools to run Age of Sigmar, Trench Crusade, StarCraft, Necromunda, or anything else. Administratum 4.0 is currently live in an opt-in beta branch, and we'll be rolling out more of it in the coming months.

There are, however, levels to this game. And at the $10 Warhound Patron level, you get expanded access to Administratum with more roster slots, more modes to run your games in, and the ability to extend $5 tier Administratrum privileges to players in your campaign who aren't signed up at that level for the duration. There are a number of reasons we actually have more subscribers at the $10 tier than at the $5 tier, and this is just one of them: This is the level where you basically get everything we have to offer. If you go higher on your pledge however -- we do have $25 and $50 tiers for those of you with discernment and taste -- you get correspondingly larger allocations of Administratum resources. If you are a maniac who has decided to run a narrative campaign for literally 300 people, the Goku S-Class Gold ULTRA tier is right for you.

That's the Pitch

We do cool shit here! We want to keep doing cool shit, more and better! Worker-owned and worker-operated bottom-up businesses like ours live and die on our valued readers, because we don't have corporate overlords to bail us out if, oh, someone goes and destroys the entire digital advertising industry because they wanted to put a demon chatbot into their search engine. Hypothetically speaking. If you think we're cool and you get value out of what we do, and any of the above sounds like it would also be cool to have in your back pocket (or front pocket, or purse, or wherever you keep your phone, which is where the Internet lives), we'd love to have you onboard.

We'll be doing more posts like these in the future, but they won't be all the same; we've got some more ideas cooking up in the oven to make your support mean even more. Look out for a big announcement coming this Thanksgiving!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Warhammer The Old World Arcane Journal - The Doom of Lord Carrard
content:
"In Ancient Nehakhara, the living must bow down before the dead." - Sir Varo of Brionne

In a move which has taken many by surprise, Games Workshop has decided we weren't done with Warhammer: The Old World in 2026 and has released another Arcane Journal following up from the River of Bones Arcane Journal last month. This book focuses on the clashes in the in the Badlands and down into the Land of the Dead as Lord Carrard takes his Questing Force to take on the forces of Nehekhara head on. As always thank you to Games Workshop for sending us a preview of this book so we could bring this to you on Pre-Order day.

In this book we have a bunch of new scenario's for you to play following through this campaign, with both Battle March and "Standard" Games of Warhammer: The Old World on display. With games of 3 various sizes (2x600, 1x1250, 1x2000) letting you follow the campaign from head to tail. Then we've got rules for expanding your Bretonnian Army around both the Questing Host Army of Infamy and then some Pledges of Honour which add another layer to this Bretonnian onion. These are then follows-on by the Khemri Dynasties which do a similar job and let you theme your lists (even more) around specific rules of Nekakhara Past.

A Tale as Old as Time

The Lore in this book follows two distinct paths. The first is, as the name suggests, Lord Carrard's journey from Bretonnian to the Boarder Princes to meet up with a disgraced Knight, Sir Lothar. From there they head down into the Badlands and as the title of the book suggests this might not go exactly to plan, but that wasn't entirely all the armies of the dead's doing.

The second trail is more background information about the Lands of the Nekekhara and it's history, going into more detail of the Gods they worshipped and the Dynasty's which formed over the years from Settra, through to Rasetra, Khetep, Lahmizzar, Lakhahaz and finally Alkhazzar followed by his descendant Alcadizaar and into what we're now in, the Seventh Dynasty, the Dynasty of the Dead.

Let's Go on a Quest

The first set of rules contained in the book are for the Questing Host Army of Infamy which sees you form an army around a host of Knights who are heading out to complete their own set tasks for their ascension. You're allowed 0-1 Baron of Prophetess per 1000 and 0-1 Outcast Wizard, full stop, it doesn't scale. In addition you're allowed Paladins, Damsels and Sergeants-at-Arms up to 50% of the force.

In Core we see 25% as a minimum requirement with 1 unit of Questing Knights per 1000 making up the core of the force with 1+ units of Knights of the Realm on Foot or Mounted bulking out the force and then Men-at-Arms, Peasant Bowmen and interesting Squires all into Core. The addition of Squires in core could prompt some Skirmishing Avoidance style lists but it's pretty hard to do that effectively when you've still got 3 units of Knights in the list at 2000pts. Special see's yet more Questing Knights alongside Mounted Yoeman, 0-1 units of Pegasus Knights (again no scaling) and 0-1 Knights Errant and 0-2 Battle Pilgrims who are both per 1000pts, again at the standard 50%.

Finally we have Rare which is up to 25% with Grail Knights and 0-1 Border Princes Brigands being the main choices here. These Questing Knights don't believe in long range fire support it seems. As usual you're allowed to upgrade a Paladin to a Battle Standard Bearer, but no Mercs have made their way into this force.

So what do you get for these restrictions? Acts of Gallantry allows Grail Reluquae within 12" of a model with the Questing Vow (who isn't fleeing) to gain the Immune to Psychology and Unbreakable special rules which are nice allowing them to really commit to being that roadblock allowing your Hammers to counter. Campaign Yoeman allows 0-1 unit of Men-at-Arms to be upgraded at +1pts to get Ws3 and the Veteran rule which seems a bargain. Holy Weapons gives all non-magical Great Weapons an additional Armour Bane up to Armour Bane (2) and Magical Attacks which is great considering last months Tomb King AoI ended up bring mass ethereal troops back into the game.

Questing Hero's grants the ability for the characters in the list who have a Chivalrous Vow to pick up a Noble Pledge of Honour and gives them way to regain back their Blessing should they ever lose it. Finally Warriors of Faith improves said blessing for any Questing Knight giving them a constant 5+ Ward, even against weaker attacks!

What I'd Do for You, My Lady

Noble Pledges of Honour follow up, these additional rules can be taken by characters (with a Vow) in this AoI or by any character with the Questing Vow in any other Bretonnian Army. Maybe we'll see some Questing Knights on the table now 'eh?

These are free upgrades and range from "Of course I'll take it" to "Please No, don't make me". Pledge of Conquest for example gives the character an additional 50VP's if it ends the battle in your opponents deployment zone, which is all upside with no real downside while Pledge of the Hunter grants your character the Monster Slayer special rule (Amazing) but they can no longer purchase a Magic Weapon (boo - but can still take Virtues) and if they fail to slay a monster during the game then your opponent gets 150VPs! As I said some of these are great and some are wild - but what's important is that they allow you to theme a list and build it more in the style you want. These will be great for campaign play when you know (with your opponent) what's coming but in matched play events some of them do feel a little bit like rolling the dice with your matchups, especially those with downsides. In those scenarios I think ones like Pledge of Wrath will just be in every army because it's something you should achieve and just give you a benefit with no real downside.

Units of Questing Knights (or any Knight unit in the Questing AoI) can also take Pledge of Honour but choose from a different list. These follow a similar trend and some give small bonuses you might remember at the end of the game while others can bite you in the backside. Pledge of Liberation grants you 50VPs if said unit is fully within your opponents Deployment Zone at the end of the game with no downside but Pledge of Honourable Warfare can end up granting your opponents 100VPs if you ever fail to win combat against opponents units with Missile Weapons, but it does give the unit Furious Charge to make that target easier.

Never-Sleeping Armies

The Tomb Kings get their next set of upgrades in this book with the Dynastic Rulers section. Here you pick an army, including any AoIs, and say it comes from a specific Dynasty. In doing so your characters get a bonus to them, but at the same time you get additional restrictions or bonuses applied to the army as a whole. I'm not a fan of the way this is presented in the book, it has you flipping back and forth between pages trying to work out what is better in combination as the character and unit amendments or restrictions are on different sections and unless I'm missing something I don't see why you couldn't put all of the rules effecting the First Dynasty for example on the same page next to each other. There are a bunch of rules here so I'm going to just break down a couple of examples.

Khemri - The First Dynasty

This gives Tomb Kings and Princes +1Ws, +1I and +1AP of any None-Magical Weapon they wield. However you can't ever decline challenges. However if you pick this then you are limited to 1 Tomb King per army and only 1 unit who's type is 'monster', 'monstrous infantry' or 'monstrous cavalry' per 1000pts. In effect meaning that you're playing with Skeleton Infantry of all it's various types and none of the newer "toys" which Tombs Kings have had added to their lists over their lifespan. However in addition to this you can upgrade any number of Skeleton Warriors to be Khemrian Spearmen for +1pts per model, this gives them Ws3 and means they have to be equipped with thrusting spears and light armour.

Zandri - The Third Dynasty

Choosing this Dynasty means that Tomb Kings, Princes and Heralds who are mounted on chariots (they don't all have to be, but if they are) gain the First Charge special rule and may re-roll any rolls of 1 when making Dangerous Terrain Tests. In addition their chariots Impact Hits also gain AP-1 which is a big impact. The restrictions around this are that 1+ character (not including the General) must be mounted on a Skeleton Chariot per 1000pts and Skeleton Chariots become 1+ per 1000pts. In addition any unit of Skeleton Chariots and Tomb Guard Chariots can be updated to be Zandrain Charioteers which means they also gain AP-1 on their Impact Hits and gain that same Dangerous Terrain test reroll, which is well worth every point of upgrade.

As you can see these are small changes, and I'm torn between them being nice little flavorful additions and yet another thing to remember at the table. I think I'm in the first camp but I know I'm going to forget something at an important point and it's going to cost me a game. It might not be till 2028, but I know it's coming at some point. For what it's worth the 2nd Dynasty - Raestra is themed around the Priests, the 4th Dynasty - Lybaras is around Archers (dangerous I know - but they have thought about it), the 5th Dynasty - Quatar is around the smaller constructs and the 6th Dynasty - Bhagar is around those shiny new Skeleton Calvary models.

If you want to have a look at the others you'll want to pick up the book when it's released but I think there's enough here for Tomb King Players to want to pick it up and benefit from some of the additional elements here without a shadow of a doubt.

Final Thoughts

I go back and forth a little over this book. The rules which are in here are 1 Army of Infamy, then some rules which I don't expect will be used loads by Bretonnian players (due to lack of Questing Knights on the table - but this might help that) and then just some bonuses for Tomb King players who want to theme an army even more than a normal AoI might do. But at the same time these rules and additions are pretty well thought through and while some of them are never going to be used in competitive play due to matchup roulette they are fun, and a lot of the time that's what certain sections of the player base (myself included) can forget. Not every new addition to the game needs to be game or Meta warping, sometimes you just want a cool addition to a new force or a new narrative hook to start a new Battle March force, and I think the Questing Force and the Dynasty's do that really well.

title: Blood Bowl Season 3: Night Goblin Team Review
content:
Welcome back, Sports Fans! Today it’s time to delve underground and see what the Old World’s nastiest, most conniving, and least trustworthy Blood Bowl teams are up to! So get ready for mayhem, violence, and more mayhem as we finally welcome Night Goblins to the pitch!

Before we dive in, we’d like to thank Games Workshop for providing us with a copy of Spike! Magazine 23 for review purposes.

Out of the deep, dark tunnels springs what has to be one of the most violent and innovative teams we’ve seen in a while. From a “fun with Blood Bowl” standpoint, this team truly has everything. Heavy hitters like Cave Squigs, Squig Wranglers, and a Troll; excellent runners and blitzers in Squig Hoppers; a new support player that everyone will immediately target every game; and a bunch of cheap yobbos to get in the way and then die. What more could you want?

While this team is certainly going to be a lot of fun, I want to stress that it is kind of a complicated mess of a Blood Bowl squad, and probably not best for a new coach. Managing Squig Rage (more on that in a bit) and the many other skills, traits, and mutations inherent in this roster is going to be tough even for veteran coaches. That being said, it’s a team of fantastic, characterful, and whimsical models, so if you are a new coach and want this team, read on, and maybe the Blood Bowl boffins can help you crack this particular nut.

In this article we’ll touch on what the players do, how to build a roster, and some general tips for playing them. Read on to get the scoop on these hellacious hooligans!

Credit: Games Workshop

Why Play Night Goblins?

Simple: you want the ability to tear your opponent’s team to shreds, and you think you can roll a bunch of 3+’s. Because, lemme tell you, if you can’t, you might be in for a long game! For some people, myself included, the wacky randomness that is part and parcel of a d6 game is a feature, not a bug. And this team leans into that hard.

Pros

  • Line of Scrimmage domination: It is possible to show up to the game with 2 ST7 Ball and Chain players, a ST5 Troll, and 2 ST4 Cave Squigs. Not even the mightiest of Chaos Renegade teams can stand up to a Night Goblin turn one without a couple of concussions.
  • Surprisingly excellent blitzers and runners: Goblin teams aren’t usually known for their top-tier positionals, Cave Squigs are some of the best natural blitzers in the game. The Cave Squig statline is nuts, and then you combine it with Frenzy, Pogo, and Jump Up and no cage is safe! Furthermore, Squig Hoppers are fast (MA7), agile, and immune to Strip Ball right out of the locker room! All you’ve got to do is manage their Squig Rage, which brings us to…
  • Squig Rage is a “negatrait”…or is it?! We’ll dive deeper into Squig Rage in just a bit, but it’s a better Animal Savagery and you can go ask coaches who use Rat Ogres how much they love that “negatrait”. Conservatively, I think half the time a Night Goblin coach fails their Squig Rage rolls, you’ll hear a derivation of “hell yeah, brother” potentially paired with a fist pump.

Cons

  • It’s never hard to get rid of Ball & Chain players: All the opponent needs is cheap Block or Wrestle players, and away those expensive, B&C players go. Also, they’re crazy unreliable even when they don’t get removed!
  • Your best players will never level: Less of a problem for tournaments, but Cave Squigs are going to be nearly impossible to skill up. Fortunately, they don’t need more skills to be good, which is good, because they’ll never get them.
  • It’s in the Bad Moon’s hands: This team is RNG personified, so you better hope the Bad Moon’s looking down on you with a smile. Is that something the Bad Moon does? I have no idea. Get good at rolling 3+’s or else you might be in for it.

The New Traits

Before we dive into the players, we’ve got to address the new traits: Squig Rage and Squig Restraint. Let’s start with the rage (emphasis in italics is mine):

  • Squig Rage (Passive): Whenever this player is activated, before declaring their action, they must roll a d6. On a 3+, the player may activate as normal. On a 1-2, the player must declare a Block Action targeting an opposition player they are Marking if able (using the Jump Up skill if applicable) - they may do this even if they have the Ball & Chain Trait and couldn’t normally do so. If the player cannot declare a Block Action against an opposition player but are adjacent to at least one team-mate, then they may choose an adjacent team-mate to be immediately Knocked Down (this will not cause a Turnover unless the chosen team-mate was holding the ball); this player may then continue their activation as normal. If this player cannot declare a Block Action against an opposition player, is not adjacent to a team-mate, or chooses not to Knock Down a team-mate, then this player becomes Distracted.

That’s a lot of words! But it boils down to: do what you want on a 3+, or get an extra block/smack your own dude if you don’t. At first glance it seems like it might be a significant limitation for the players that have it, but let us, for a moment, consider the Rat Ogre. Rat Ogres have Animal Savagery, which is generally considered to be one of the best negatraits, as it is can be unfailable simply by sitting a yobbo next to the Rat Ogre before they activate. Then, even if the Rat Ogre’s coach fails the roll, the Rat Ogre punches its friend and goes about their business as normal. So take that and add an extra Block Action to the mix. In some cases, the Night Goblin coach wants to fail the Squig Rage roll to get multiple blocks! Furthermore, this test is made before the player declares an action, meaning you can’t waste your Blitz on a Squig Rager like you can with other negatraits! Further-further-more a Ball & Chain player can make regular Blocks when they fail their Squig Rage roll, which is something they normally cannot do! And, finally, all the players with Squig Rage on the team are capable blockers, so even if you are forced to make Block Actions with them, you ain’t even gonna be mad!

That was a lot of words again. I’m sorry. But it’s important to point this stuff out to make the following point: I’m not even sure Squig Rage is a negatrait! I think a Night Goblin coach wants to be failing this roll probably 50% of the time! It can even make Ball & Chain players less random somehow! I think you can tell that I’m pretty excited about this trait. I think it’s flavorful, fun, and, importantly, very good. I can’t wait to get this team on the pitch!

Ok, with all that said, let’s take a look at Squig Restraint.

  • Squig Restrait (Passive): Team-mates within 3 squares of a Standing player with this trait do not roll for their Squig Rage Trait at the start of their activation and may activate as normal.

This one’s a lot easier to parse, thank Sigmar! If at any point you were worried about making those all-important Squig Rage rolls, you can just ignore them with a well-placed Squig Herder. Simple as. You should note two things, though: it’s a Passive trait meaning that if they are standing and Distracted, it is still in effect (a use case here would be if the Squig Herder got Hypo-Gazed). And lastly, this trait fully overrides Squig Rage. You may not choose to roll the Squig Rage check if the Squig Restraint player is within range, even if you really want to.

The Players

In the tradition of the “regular” goblin team, this team has a big selection of special positions to choose from. This team will lean heavily into the madcap fun of RNG, but has some really good statlines and skill pieces that, in the hands of either very lucky or experienced coaches, could cause some serious problems for their opponents.

Each entry has a bolded portion at the top, and here’s how to decipher it:

  • The 1st part is the name of the player. Example: Night Goblin Lineman. In brackets, the first value is price. Example: 45k = 45,000 gp.
  • Then, we have skill access with primary/secondary. Example: GS/AD means General and Strength skills for primary and Agility and Devious skills for secondary.
  • Skills are abbreviated: A  = Agility, D = Devious, G = General, M = Mutation, P = Passing, S = Strength
  • Next is the number you can take on your team. Example: 0-16 means you can take between 0 and 16 of this type of player.
  • Finally, we have the faction and position of the player. Example: Night Goblin linemen have the faction keyword Goblin, and the position keyword Lineman.
Credit: Games Workshop

Night Goblin Lineman [45k, AD/GPS, 0-16, Goblin, Lineman]: The only differences between these guys and their counterparts on the regular Goblin team are that Night Goblin Line-os come with 2 extra skills: Taunt and Shadowing, and are 5k gp more expensive. My take here is that these guys are pretty good! Taunt is a legit good skill to have on what is basically a speed bump character, as it will allow the Night Gobbo to lock down much more expensive players very easily, especially big blockers who don’t have Block or Tackle. Shadowing will almost never matter, and when it does, you’ll fail the roll anyways. 5k more isn’t my favorite, but I’d say it’s worth it to have your linemen control where the opponent can move their players.

Credit: Games Workshop

Squig Herder [55k, AD/GPS, 0-2, Goblin, Special]: The reason you take these guys is the ever-important Squig Restraint trait, which I’ve written about above. Stat-wise, they’re Goblins with worse Passing. Apart from that, they drop Shadowing, Taunt, and Right Stuff to pick up Fend and Disturbing Presence (along with the aforementioned Squig Restraint). This player is tricky, because you need them to smooth out the variance in your team, but they’re also easily removed and massive targets. And besides giving you access to Squig Restraint, they don’t really do anything else. Everyone is going to need to take at least 1, but then you have to work out how to protect them during the game. Good luck with that!

Squig Hopper [80k, AD/GPS, 0-2, Goblin, Squig, Special]: Now we’re talking! MA7, ST3, AG 3+ with Dodge, Jump Up, Monstrous Mouth, Pogo, and Squig Rage. That’s quite the package! These guys are obviously your best candidates for running the ball, but at ST3, they make a pretty good blitzer, too! AV8+ isn’t good for hanging and banging, but pogo-ing over defenders to sneak a cheeky blitz in and maybe even pick up the ball afterwards isn’t nothing. Monstrous Mouth is funny here because it’s obviously great to negate Strip Ball, but the only time you’d actually want to chomp someone is if they’re ST2 or lower. Because, again, AV8+. Squig Rage here is the only real impediment, but a thoughtfully placed Squig Herder or a sacrificial lineman will mitigate that rule quite nicely. I quite like this player and they’ll obviously be a Night Goblin mainstay.

Squig Wrangler [70k, DS/AG, 0-2, Goblin, Squig, Special]: ST7, Ball & Chain, and no Secret Weapon! Apparently a leashed squig being swung around as a weapon is a legal play in the Blood Bowl rulebook. Or maybe it’s an Air Bud situation where there is no rule expressly prohibiting using a squig as a weapon. Either way, the Squig Wrangler is one of the Night Goblin Team’s biggest draws. You can take 2 of them at team creation and combine them with a Troll for one of the scariest front lines in the game. But just remember: they can absolutely whiff every time they activate and if your friends don’t know how to play around them, trust me, they’ll figure it out. Personally I’m not a huge fan of Ball & Chain players who don’t come with Mighty Blow, so I think the 70k price tag is a lot to ask here. I’m sure a lot of you will windmill slam 2 of these into every roster every time, and for that I salute you. But with random, slow movement and the fact that they’re extremely easy to remove, I wouldn’t bet the game on them.

Cave Squig [85k, -/ADGS, 0-2, Squig, Special]: Here’s a player that I will bet the game on: the Cave Squig! Y’all, these big, round, bitey belligerents are not to be underestimated! With ST4, MA6, Pogo, and Frenzy, no cage is safe! Cave Squigs make fantastic blitzers right out of the box, and every roster will begin by taking 2. They even have AG3+ meaning that they’re not easy to pin down like a lot of ST4 players are! This is another player where you kinda want to fail your Squig Rage checks every now and then, as it will net you extra blocks. The only drawback here is that animalistic Cave Squigs don’t have any primary skills. This means that they’ll take forever to level, but the good news is that these bad biters don’t need any new skills to be great.

Blood Bowl Goblin Troll by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

Trained Troll [115k, S/AGP, 0-1, Troll, Big Guy]: This is the exact same Troll from the Goblin or Snotling teams, and everyone knows exactly what to expect here. I think they have a special place in this roster as your linemen all come with Right Stuff, and you probably want to be able to take advantage of that with your Throw Team-mate troll. We love a cheap Big Guy.

Starting League Rosters

Let’s start with the 1-box, no-Troll look, as it’s the most accessible way to play this team:

  • 2 Cave Squigs
  • 2 Squig Wranglers
  • 2 Squig Hoppers
  • 2 Squig Herders
  • 4 Night Goblin Linemen
  • 3 Rerolls
  • 970,000 gp

You could drop the 3rd RR for 2 more Night Goblin Linemen if you wanted to, but I think this team is thirsty for RRs and linemen are going to be trivial to pick up during league play. I feel like this team really wants a Troll to anchor the line, but this starting roster is 100% playable, and will probably be a ton of madcap fun.

Ok, let’s get a Troll in here and see what we come up with:

  • 1 Troll
  • 2 Cave Squigs
  • 2 Squig Wranglers
  • 2 Squig Hoppers
  • 1 Squig Herder
  • 4 Linemen
  • 2 Rerolls
  • 960,000 gp

This is your “go big or go home” roster with 2 Wranglers to cause chaos on the line with the Troll. Now, I’m a noted Ball & Chain hater, as they’re slow, random, and easy to remove, but if you’re into that kind of mess, then you’ll love the above roster.

I think the following roster is probably what I’d bring to game 1 of a league:

  • 1 Troll
  • 2 Cave Squigs
  • 1 Squig Wrangler
  • 2 Squig Hoppers
  • 2 Squig Herders
  • 5 Linemen
  • 2 Rerolls
  • 990,000 gp

This list gets you an extra body instead of the 2nd Wrangler, which you’ll probably need because there’s a lot of AV8+ on this team! And a 70k player isn’t exactly a big lift once the league gets going, so you can get that 2nd Wrangler sharpish.

Credit: Games Workshop

League Progression

You’re going to have to balance having enough players on the roster to complete games with not letting your TV get too bloated. It’ll be a tough line to walk, so don’t let your linemen accrue too many upgrades!

  • Night Goblin Linemen: I see these guys as speed bumps and foulers. Speed bumps don’t need (and shouldn’t get!) and upgrades, and foulers just need one or two of the good Devious skills: Dirty Player, Lone Fouler, Quick Fouler, and Sneaky Git. If you get a Lineman up to 6 SPP give them Dirty Player, but if you’re gonna play the random game, I’d fire anyone who didn’t randomly roll up one of those four skills and rehire a new line-o.
  • Squig Herder: These guys don’t really need skills to do what they’re there for, which is to stand around, so I would never select them for MVP or intentionally try and score with them. I probably wouldn’t even level one if they did have enough SPP, honestly. They just don’t need it, and your team doesn’t need the extra TV. But if you are going to level them, I suggest something that will help keep them alive or give them extra mobility. Sprint or Block come to mind.
  • Squig Hopper: Hoppers are your ball carriers, so they want the good ball carrier stuff: Sprint, Block, Sure Hands, Sidestep. You’ll probably end up scoring with these guys quite a bit, so secondary skills are definitely on the menu.
  • Squig Wrangler: Mighty Blow! You want those ST7 hits removing players if at all possible, and ol’, reliable Mighty Blow is there for you. If you manage to get 2 on one of these guys, Brawler is a good bet.
  • Cave Squig: With only secondary skill choices and No Ball, progression is going to be slow with Cave Squigs. But these are your ball-hawks, so treat them like so. They come with Jump Up, so Wrestle is an obvious choice here. After that, Tackle and Strip Ball make a lot of sense. Pro is probably nice here, too, to help mitigate Squig Rage.
  • Troll: In Guard we trust! After that, I like Strong Arm for cheeky Throw Team-mate action. Also, Bullseye is really good for that, too.

Tournament Rosters

For this, we’re going to assume 1.1 million gp for roster creation. However, I don’t know what tier this team is going to end up in. I’d err on the safe side and call them tier 3, but they’re just goblins at the end of the day, so they might end up in tier 4. So, for this exercise, I am assuming a skill pack with 8 skill points and a max of 2 secondary skills available.

  • 4 Night Goblin Linemen
  • 2 Squig Herders
  • 2 Squig Hoppers w/ Sprint
  • 2 Squig Wranglers w/ Mighty Blow
  • 1 Cave Squig w/ Wrestle
  • 1 Cave Squig w/ Tackle
  • 1 Troll
  • 3 RRs
  • 1,085,000 gp
Credit: Games Workshop

General Tactics

The number 1 rule for playing Night Goblins is: Don’t fail your Squig Rage rolls!

But seriously, you’re playing a goblin team, so Fouling every turn is an absolute must. After that, you’ve got to be very careful with positioning your Night Goblins. You’re going to have at least 5 players on your team who want a babysitter or a Squig Herder nearby for every activation. Well-placed Herders will be critical on offense to keep your Hoppers from futzing around. And with 2 Ball & Chain players (probably) you might have fewer than normal mobile dudes running around to help you set cages, so don’t be scared to follow your whirling dervishes down the pitch. Cave Squigs are your absolute best players, but they’re only AV9+, so you can be too reckless with them. At some point you’re going to want to cage dive with them, but you need to Mark the entire cage to avoid getting Frenzy trapped.

This team has a lot of potential to be a problem, but it’s goblins with 3+ gates all around, so play patiently and expect to fail: position your players for maximum impact when you do. Don’t go for the big blocks early in the turn, move those gobbos around first in case you turn it over.

Final Thoughts

I think GW is really on to something with this team. It might not be the most approachable or strongest team out there, but it has a sky-high skill ceiling and looks to be a ton of fun, even in a loss. However, I wouldn’t recommend this team to a new player because it is extremely complicated with interlocking rules and fragile tech pieces. That being said, I am pre-ordering this team immediately and hope to run it early next year in local leagues! Thanks for reading!
